content: In settings where a child is the offspring of an individual with HIV or tuberculosis (TB), the child is at a significantly elevated risk of acquiring both HIV and TB infections. Detailed information on this topic is available in Chapter 6. Recommendation 22: In regions with high HIV prevalence, all household members and close contacts of individuals with TB should receive counseling and testing for HIV. This is a strong recommendation, although the quality of evidence supporting it is very low. This guidance is based on recommendations for investigating contacts of individuals with infectious TB in lowand middle-income countries. Recommendation 23: In areas with low HIV prevalence, household and close contacts of TB patients who exhibit symptoms consistent with TB disease may be offered HIV counseling and testing as part of their clinical evaluation. This is a conditional recommendation, also supported by very low-quality evidence. Recommendation 24: All household contacts of an index case who is a person living with HIV (PLHIV) should be counseled and tested for HIV. This is a strong recommendation, despite the very low quality of evidence. Implementation Considerations for Managing Child Contacts in National Tuberculosis Programs (NTPs): While most NTPs recommend screening and managing close contacts of TB cases, these practices are rarely implemented in lowand middle-income settings, where the majority of childhood TB cases occur. There is no need to establish separate infrastructure for contact screening and management; these activities can be integrated into existing NTP structures and supported by current specialist resources. A symptom-based screening approach enables contact management at the community level without requiring additional resources. All NTPs should have written guidelines for contact investigation, including standardized protocols and procedures to improve efficiency and uniformity. These protocols should outline priorities for contact investigation, define the roles and responsibilities of health workers, and provide guidance on data collection and recording. Sample forms for contact investigation and household TB contact screening are available in other WHO guidelines. TB Infection Control: Communities have the right to safe healthcare environments, free from the risk of TB transmission, and healthcare workers are entitled to a safe working environment. The association of TB with HIV, along with the emergence of multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) and extensively drug-resistant TB (XDR-TB), underscores the growing importance of TB infection control. Community awareness campaigns can help reduce TB transmission, promote sustainable behavioral changes, and minimize stigma associated with identifying potentially infectious individuals. Communities play a critical role in preventing TB transmission in congregate settings and households. WHO Guidelines on TB Infection Control: WHO has published guidelines to prevent TB transmission in healthcare facilities, congregate settings, and households. Effective TB infection control requires actions such as involving patients and communities in advocacy campaigns, developing and regularly reviewing infection control plans, ensuring safe sputum collection, promoting cough etiquette, triaging individuals with presumptive TB, ensuring rapid diagnosis and treatment, improving ventilation, protecting healthcare workers, and monitoring infection control practices. Nosocomial TB Transmission Risks: Other contributing factors include poor adherence to TB treatment, weak healthcare systems, limited implementation of antiretroviral therapy (ART) and isoniazid preventive therapy (IPT), staff shortages, inadequate staff education, and patient-related factors such as poverty and stigma. Children are particularly vulnerable to TB transmission in healthcare facilities, especially infants and young children living with HIV. Individuals with presumptive TB should not share waiting areas with immunocompromised children, such as those attending immunization clinics or HIV clinics. Children with smear-positive TB should be isolated to prevent transmission. TB in Children Living with HIV: This risk is influenced by the degree of immune suppression. All children living with HIV in TB-endemic settings should be regularly screened for TB during healthcare visits. Evaluation should aim to identify those requiring anti-TB treatment or IPT. The clinical presentation of TB in children often overlaps with other conditions such as pneumonia, HIV, and malnutrition, making diagnosis challenging. Symptom-based screening is recommended, as children without symptoms such as poor weight gain, fever, or cough are unlikely to have TB disease. Children living with HIV who are close contacts of active TB cases should begin IPT regardless of age if TB disease is excluded. BCG Vaccination: BCG vaccination should not be administered to infants or children with known HIV infection due to the risk of disseminated BCG disease. Treatment of TB in Children Living with HIV: Children with suspected or confirmed pulmonary TB or tuberculous lymphadenitis in high HIV prevalence settings should not be treated with intermittent regimens (e.g., twiceor thrice-weekly doses). Instead, a six-month regimen consisting of a two-month intensive phase with four drugs (HRZE) followed by a four-month continuation phase with two drugs (HR) is recommended. Children should be assessed two weeks after starting treatment and then reviewed monthly to monitor symptoms, weight, adherence, and adverse events. Dosages of anti-TB drugs should be adjusted based on weight gain. Most children living with HIV respond well to this regimen if they adhere to therapy. However, treatment failure may occur due to non-compliance, drug-resistant TB, or misdiagnosis. Children who successfully complete TB treatment should receive an additional six months of isoniazid. Preventing TB in Children Living with HIV: All children living with HIV should be screened for TB, and all children with TB should be offered HIV testing and counseling in high HIV prevalence settings. Children living with HIV who are household contacts of infectious TB cases should be evaluated for TB disease and either treated or given preventive therapy. Innovative approaches are needed to identify co-infected children and prevent disease, requiring integration of TB and HIV services.
